slides.title: Spoken Tutorial on Introduction to API
slides.narration: Welcome to this Spoken Tutorial on **Introduction to API**.

slides.title: Learning Objectives
slides.narration:
In this tutorial, you will learn,

• Define what an **Application Programming Interface** (**API**) is.
• Explain the role of **API keys** in secure access.
• Describe the process of sending requests and receiving responses via an **API**.
• Apply the concept of **API** as a connector in application development.

slides.title: System Requirements
slides.narration: Here I am using a browser on a computer or mobile.

slides.title: Prerequisites
slides.narration: To follow this tutorial, you should have knowledge of Episode 1: **Basics of Python**.

slides.title: What is an API? A Digital Connector
slides.narration:
Have you ever wondered how different apps talk to each other?
An **API**, or **Application Programming Interface**, is like a digital waiter.
Imagine you are at a restaurant and place an order.
The waiter takes your order, goes to the kitchen, and brings back your food.
Similarly, an **API** takes your software's request to another service.
It then brings back the data or result you asked for.
This allows applications to communicate and share data securely.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing API as a digital waiter connecting different applications

slides.title: Main Demo: Vague Request
slides.narration:
Now, let's look at how we make requests.
Imagine you walk into a restaurant and simply say, 'I want food'.
What do you think the waiter will bring you?
This is like sending a vague, unstructured request to an **API**.
The **API** might not understand or give you something unexpected.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'I want food...'

slides.title: Main Demo: Improved Request
slides.narration:
Now, consider a different approach.
What if you say, 'I want a large pepperoni pizza with extra cheese'?
This request is specific and clear, right?
This is similar to sending a structured request to an **API**.
A structured request tells the **API** exactly what you need.
This ensures the **API** understands and fulfills your request precisely.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'I want a large pepperoni pizza with extra cheese...'

slides.title: Main Demo: Vague vs. Improved
slides.narration:
See the difference?
Comparing the vague and improved requests shows us something important.
Structured communication is key for efficient and accurate responses.
This applies directly to how we interact with **APIs**.
slides.image_prompt: Side-by-side: vague request output vs improved request output

slides.title: Securing Access with API Keys
slides.narration:
But how do **APIs** know who is asking for what?
**API keys** are unique identifiers.
They act like a digital key for authentication.
This controls who can access specific **API** services.
It also defines what actions they are allowed to perform.
It's essential for keeping data and services secure.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing a digital key unlocking access to API services

slides.title: Anatomy of an API Request
slides.narration:
Now, let's look at the structure of an **API** request.
Every request has an **endpoint**, which is like the address or **URL**.
Then there's a **method**, such as **GET** to retrieve data or **POST** to send data.
**Headers** provide important metadata about the request.
Sometimes, there's also a **body**, which contains the actual data payload.
Understanding these parts helps you build effective requests.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing the components of an API request: endpoint, method, headers, and body

slides.title: Understanding API Responses
slides.narration:
Once an **API** processes your request, it sends back a **response**.
This **response** usually includes a **status code**.
**200 OK** means success, while **404 Not Found** means there was an error.
The **response** also contains the data you asked for.
This data is typically in a structured format like **JSON** or **XML**.
Learning to interpret these responses is crucial for development.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing an API response with status codes and data in JSON format

slides.title: Putting it Together: An API Workflow Example
slides.narration:
Let's put all these pieces together with an example.
Imagine an application wants to use an **AI** service.
First, the application sends a request with its unique **API key**.
The **API** receives and processes this request securely.
Finally, the **API** returns the desired **AI**-generated response to the application.
This complete cycle shows a typical **API** workflow.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing a complete API workflow: application sending request with API key, API processing, and returning AI-generated response

slides.title: Summary
slides.narration:
Let us summarize what we learned.
We explored what **APIs** are and their role as digital connectors.
We also understood how **API keys** secure access to services.
Finally, we looked at the complete **API** request and response cycle.

slides.title: Assignment
slides.narration:
Now as an assignment,
Try to identify three common applications you use daily.
Think about which of these likely rely on **APIs** for their functionality.
Compare the results.
